prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Animula, vagula, blandula. Life! I know not what thou art, But know that thou and I must part; And when, or how, or where we met, I own to me’s a secret yet. But this I know, when thou art fled, Where’er they lay these limbs, this head, No clod so valueless shall be, As all that then remains of me. O whither, whither dost thou fly, Where bend unseen thy trackless course, And in this strange divorce, Ah tell where I must seek this compound I? To the vast ocean of empyreal flame, From whence thy essence came, Dost thou thy flight pursue, when freed From matter’s base encumbering weed? Or dost thou, hid from sight, Wait, like some spell-bound knight, Through blank oblivious years th’ appointed hour, To break thy trance and reassume thy power? Yet canst thou without thought or feeling be? O say what art thou, when no more thou ’rt thee? Life! we’ve been long together, Through pleasant and through cloudy weather; ’Tis hard to part when friends are dear; Perhaps ’t will cost a sigh, a tear; Then steal away, give little warning, Choose thine own time; Say not Good night, but in some brighter clime Bid me Good morning.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Animula, Life, But

outputs.L1:
Animula, vagula, blandula.

Life! I know not what thou art,  
Yet know that thou and I must part;  
And when, or how, or where we met,  
I own remains a secret yet.  

But this I know: when thou art fled,  
Where’er they lay these limbs, this head,  
No clod so valueless shall be  
As all that then remains of me.  

O whither, whither dost thou fly?  
Where bends, unseen, thy trackless course?  
And in this strange divorce,  
Ah, tell me where I must seek this compound I.  

To the vast ocean of empyreal flame,  
From whence thy essence came,  
Dost thou thy flight pursue, when freed  
From matter’s base, encumbering weed?  

Or dost thou, hidden from sight,  
Wait, like some spell-bound knight,  
Through blank, oblivious years, the appointed hour  
To break thy trance and reassume thy power?  

Yet canst thou be without thought or feeling?  
O say, what art thou, when no more thou art thee?  

Life! We have been long together,  
Through pleasant and through cloudy weather;  
’Tis hard to part when friends are dear—  
Perhaps ’twill cost a sigh, a tear.  

Then steal away; give little warning;  
Choose thine own time.  
Say not “Good night,” but in some brighter clime  
Bid me “Good morning.”
outputs.L2:
Little wandering, gentle soul—  
Life! I do not understand what you are,  
Yet I know that you and I are bound to separate.  
When we first joined, or how, or in what place,  
I admit remains a mystery to me.  

But this much I understand: once you have gone,  
Wherever they place these arms, this body, this head,  
No lump of earth will be so worthless  
As what is left of me then.  

Oh, where, where do you go?  
What invisible, unmarked path do you take?  
And in this strange separation,  
Tell me—where am I to search for this blended self?  

Do you rise toward the boundless sea  
Of heavenly fire  
From which your being first came,  
Once you are released  
From the low, burdensome clothing of matter?  

Or do you remain concealed from view,  
Waiting, like an enchanted knight,  
Through empty years of forgetfulness  
For the destined moment  
When you may awaken and regain your strength?  

And yet—can you exist without thought or feeling?  
Tell me: what are you  
When you are no longer yourself?  

Life, you and I have kept company for many years,  
In happy days and in dark ones too.  
It is painful to part from a beloved companion;  
Perhaps it will bring a sigh, perhaps a tear.  

So slip away quietly, with little notice,  
At whatever hour you choose.  
Do not say, “Good night,”  
But, in some fairer world,  
Greet me instead with, “Good morning.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects deeply on the mystery of life, recognizing that its true nature is beyond human understanding. Life is presented as something intimate and essential, yet also strange and unknowable. The speaker admits that they do not know what life really is, where it comes from, or how it became joined with the physical body. This uncertainty gives the poem a thoughtful and philosophical tone, as it explores questions that have no simple answers.

The poem strongly emphasizes the difference between the living body and the body after life has departed. While life remains within it, the body has movement, warmth, feeling, and meaning. Once life leaves, however, the body becomes empty and worthless, reduced to mere matter. Without the presence of life or the soul, the physical form loses all importance. This contrast highlights the idea that the body depends entirely on life for its value and vitality.

The speaker also wonders what happens to life or the soul after death. They imagine several possibilities, but none can be known with certainty. Perhaps life returns to its divine source, rejoining the power that first created it. Perhaps it enters a state of silence, darkness, or oblivion, waiting for some unknown future. These reflections show the speaker’s desire to understand death, while also accepting that the fate of the soul remains a mystery.

Another important question in the poem is whether life can continue to exist after leaving the body if it no longer has thought, feeling, memory, or identity. The speaker asks whether existence without consciousness can truly be called life at all. If the soul loses its sense of self, its emotions, and its awareness, then it becomes difficult to imagine what kind of existence remains. Through these questions, the poem examines the connection between life, consciousness, and personal identity.

Although the speaker is troubled by these uncertainties, they gradually move toward acceptance. They acknowledge the pain of parting from life, recognizing that death involves loss and separation. Yet the poem does not end in complete despair. Instead, the speaker expresses hope that death may not be simple extinction, but a passage into a new and brighter form of existence. In this way, the poem balances fear and sorrow with faith and hope, suggesting that beyond the darkness of death there may be an awakening into greater light.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the mystery of life, death, and the soul’s destiny through an intimate address to “Life” itself. By speaking to Life as though it were a close companion, the speaker gives abstract ideas a personal and emotional force. Life is not treated merely as a condition of existence, but as something familiar, beloved, and difficult to leave. This apostrophe creates a tone of tenderness and reflection, suggesting that the speaker is already contemplating separation from the world and wondering what lies beyond it.

Throughout the poem, the speaker turns to a series of questioning images in order to express uncertainty about death and the afterlife. These questions do not receive clear, rational answers; instead, they reveal the limits of human knowledge. The speaker wonders what becomes of the soul when earthly life ends, whether death is an extinction, a sleep, or a passage into another state of being. The repeated questioning gives the poem a meditative quality, as if the speaker is searching for comfort while standing at the edge of the unknown.

At the same time, the poem does not present death as purely terrifying. Although parting from life is sorrowful, the speaker’s grief is softened by the possibility of spiritual renewal. The idea of awakening in a “brighter clime” suggests that death may lead not to darkness, but to a more radiant and peaceful existence. This image transforms death from a final loss into a kind of transition, a movement from the imperfect world into a higher and more blessed realm.

In this way, the poem balances sadness with consolation. It acknowledges the pain of leaving life behind and the uncertainty that surrounds the soul’s fate, but it also offers hope that death may bring awakening rather than destruction. The final effect is gentle and reassuring: life is precious, parting from it is painful, yet the belief in a brighter existence beyond death gives meaning and comfort to the human experience.
outputs.L5:
**Animula, Life, But**

Animula means “little soul,” a small and tender word for the quiet inner life we carry through the world. It is the part of us that wonders, remembers, fears, hopes, and searches for meaning even in ordinary moments.

Life is never only one thing. It is joy, but also sorrow. It is movement, but also waiting. It gives us beginnings, but it also teaches us endings. We make plans, but life often answers in unexpected ways. Still, the animula within us continues to listen, to learn, and to grow.

But perhaps that is the beauty of being alive: we are fragile, but not empty; uncertain, but not without direction. Our little soul travels through time, gathering light from love, pain, memory, and change. And even when life feels confusing, the animula remains—a quiet flame reminding us that we are more than what happens to us.
